stem: A postoperative client has an order that includes incentive spirometry. Which nursing plan is most consistent with current AARC guidance?

options.A: Use incentive spirometry as ordered together with coached deep breathing and coughing, early mobilization, and adequate analgesia rather than using the device alone.
options.B: Use incentive spirometry at scheduled intervals and reduce other lung-expansion measures once the client demonstrates correct technique with the device.
options.C: Keep the client in bed between spirometry sessions so the device can serve as the primary prophylactic measure while postoperative pain is treated.
options.D: Stop the incentive-spirometry order and use deep-breathing exercises instead, because AARC guidance considers the two approaches interchangeable in all patients.

rationale: The American Association for Respiratory Care guideline states that incentive spirometry alone is not recommended as routine preoperative or postoperative prophylaxis. When incentive spirometry is used, AARC recommends combining it with deep-breathing techniques, directed coughing, early mobilization, and optimal analgesia. AARC also notes that deep-breathing exercises may provide similar perioperative benefit, but that does not make the approaches universally interchangeable or authorize the nurse to discontinue an existing order independently. The 2013 AARC nonpharmacologic airway-clearance guideline likewise does not recommend routine prophylactic incentive spirometry and does recommend early mobility and ambulation for postoperative clients. Therefore A is correct. B incorrectly substitutes the device for complementary measures after technique is learned, C makes bed rest and incentive spirometry the primary strategy, and D overgeneralizes the deep-breathing evidence and independently stops an ordered intervention.
educational_objective: When incentive spirometry is ordered after surgery, use it as one component of multimodal pulmonary care with deep breathing, coughing, early mobilization, and adequate analgesia rather than as stand-alone prophylaxis.
source_document_title: AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Incentive Spirometry: 2011; AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Effectiveness of Nonpharmacologic Airway Clearance Therapies in Hospitalized Patients
source_version_date: Incentive Spirometry guideline published 2011 and still listed by AARC in 2026 under Expert Panel Reference-Based Guidelines; nonpharmacologic airway-clearance guideline published 2013 and listed by AARC in 2026 under Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines
source_locator: Incentive Spirometry: 2011 > Recommendations 14.1–14.5: incentive spirometry alone is not recommended for routine preoperative/postoperative prevention; when used, combine with deep breathing, directed coughing, early mobilization, and optimal analgesia; deep-breathing exercises may provide similar perioperative benefit; routine prophylactic use after upper-abdominal surgery or CABG is not recommended. Effectiveness of Nonpharmacologic Airway Clearance Therapies in Hospitalized Patients > Postoperative Patients > Recommendations Supported by Low-Level Evidence: routine prophylactic incentive spirometry is not recommended; early mobility and ambulation are recommended to reduce postoperative complications and promote airway clearance. AARC Clinical Practice Guidelines index: Incentive Spirometry (2011) remains listed as an Expert Panel Reference-Based Guideline and the 2013 airway-clearance guideline remains listed as evidence-based guidance.
source_claim_supported: AARC guidance supports incentive spirometry, when used postoperatively, as part of a broader lung-expansion strategy rather than routine stand-alone prophylaxis, with early mobilization and adequate analgesia retained as complementary measures.

supporting_sources.document_title: AARC Clinical Practice Guideline: Effectiveness of Nonpharmacologic Airway Clearance Therapies in Hospitalized Patients
supporting_sources.version_date: Published 2013; current on AARC guideline index in 2026
supporting_sources.locator: Postoperative Patients > Recommendations Supported by Low-Level Evidence: incentive spirometry is not recommended for routine prophylactic use in postoperative patients; early mobility and ambulation are recommended to reduce postoperative complications and promote airway clearance.
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Postoperative pulmonary-complication prevention should not rely on routine incentive spirometry alone and should preserve early mobility.

supporting_sources.locator: Expert Panel Reference-Based Guidelines: Incentive Spirometry (2011). Evidence-Based Clinical Practice Guidelines: Effectiveness of Nonpharmacologic Airway Clearance Therapies in Hospitalized Patients (2013).
supporting_sources.claim_supported: Both cited AARC guidance documents remain actively listed rather than appearing in the retired-guideline section.

blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Physiological Adaptation, printed pp. 46–47: related activity statements include provide postoperative care and provide pulmonary hygiene (e.g., chest physiotherapy, incentive spirometry); detailed content again includes provide pulmonary hygiene and provide postoperative care, plus evaluate client response to surgery and treatment goals.
blueprint_topic: Physiological Adaptation — postoperative pulmonary hygiene and multimodal care when incentive spirometry is ordered
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four plans to eliminate the uniquely-long keyed answer, preserved AARC's distinction between incentive spirometry as an adjunct versus routine stand-alone prophylaxis, and remapped the item from Basic Care and Comfort to Physiological Adaptation because the 2026 NCSBN Test Plan explicitly lists postoperative care and pulmonary hygiene including incentive spirometry there.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Postoperative pulmonary hygiene — incentive spirometry within multimodal care
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies that incentive spirometry is already ordered and asks how to integrate it into current postoperative care without implying universal prophylactic benefit.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS — directly follows AARC recommendation 14.2 and retains early mobility and analgesia; uniquely best.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — correct technique matters, but successful device use does not justify reducing the complementary lung-expansion and mobility measures AARC pairs with incentive spirometry.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — pain treatment is appropriate, but bed rest conflicts with AARC postoperative guidance supporting early mobility and makes incentive spirometry the primary prophylactic measure.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS as distractor — AARC notes similar benefit from deep breathing in some perioperative evidence, but this does not make the interventions interchangeable in every client or authorize unilateral discontinuation of an existing order.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — A is the only option that both respects the existing order and applies the guideline's multimodal strategy without overclaiming the device's independent benefit.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — B de-emphasizes complementary measures, C substitutes device use for mobility, and D overgeneralizes evidence and stops the order independently.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — all choices are comparable in length and specificity and the keyed answer is no longer uniquely long.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — NCSBN Physiological Adaptation explicitly names postoperative care and pulmonary hygiene including incentive spirometry.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether D could be defended because AARC states deep breathing may provide similar benefit; that statement is not a universal substitution rule, while recommendation 14.2 specifically directs combining incentive spirometry with deep breathing, coughing, mobilization, and analgesia when the device is used. A remains uniquely best.
